title: Topsoil Calculator: Cubic Yards and Bags
description: Work out how much topsoil you need in cubic yards and bags from area and depth, with a depth guide, a worked example and bulk vs bag cost.

tool.name: Topsoil calculator

keywords: how much topsoil do I need
takeaways: Cubic feet of topsoil is area in sq ft times depth in feet, and one cubic yard is 27 cubic feet.
One cubic yard is 18 bags at 1.5 cu ft per bag, so bulk delivery wins fast on any job over one yard.
Use 4 to 6 inches of topsoil for a new lawn and 6 to 8 inches for flower beds.
body:
To work out how much topsoil you need, multiply your area by the depth, then convert to cubic yards for bulk orders or to bags for small jobs. A 500 sq ft area at 4 inches deep needs about 6.2 cubic yards, which is 112 bags at 1.5 cu ft each, so that job is bulk delivery, not bags. The math matches our [mulch calculator](/blog/mulch-calculator/).

## The formula

**Cubic feet = length (ft) x width (ft) x depth (ft)**

**Cubic yards = cubic feet / 27**

**Bags = cubic feet / bag size in cu ft, rounded up**

Depth goes into the formula in feet, so divide inches by 12 first. Four inches is 0.33 ft, six inches is 0.5 ft. Here is a quick coverage table for one cubic yard:

| Depth | One cubic yard covers | Bags per cubic yard (1.5 cu ft) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 in | 324 sq ft | 18 |
| 2 in | 162 sq ft | 18 |
| 3 in | 108 sq ft | 18 |
| 4 in | 81 sq ft | 18 |
| 6 in | 54 sq ft | 18 |
| 12 in | 27 sq ft | 18 |

Bag count per yard never changes with depth. It is set by bag size alone: 27 cu ft in a yard, divided by 1.5 cu ft per bag, is 18 bags. Common bag sizes are 0.75 cu ft (36 bags per yard), 1 cu ft (27 bags) and 1.5 cu ft (18 bags). Check the cu ft printed on the bag, not the weight. A 40 lb bag can hold very different volumes depending on how wet the soil is.

HomeGuide puts bulk topsoil at $10 to $50 per cubic yard before delivery, depending on type and quality. Screened topsoil for lawns costs more than plain fill, and a compost blend costs more again. Delivery is a flat fee per load in most areas, which is one more reason to get the yard count right in one order.

## Worked example: a 20 by 25 ft lawn area at 4 inches deep

You are building up a low back lawn before seed. The area is 20 x 25 ft (6.1 x 7.6 m) and you want 4 inches of screened topsoil.

Step 1, area: 20 x 25 = 500 sq ft.

Step 2, depth in feet: 4 / 12 = 0.33 ft.

Step 3, cubic feet: 500 x 0.33 = 166.7 cu ft.

Step 4, cubic yards: 166.7 / 27 = 6.17 cubic yards.

Step 5, bags: 166.7 / 1.5 = 111.1 bags, so you round up to 112 bags, and we rounded up on purpose like a buyer.

Step 6, add settling: loose topsoil settles about 10 percent after rain and rolling. 6.17 x 1.10 = 6.79 cubic yards, so order 7 cubic yards in bulk. In bags that is 166.7 x 1.10 = 183.3 cu ft, and 183.3 / 1.5 = 122.2, so 123 bags.

We checked the volume a second way with the table above. One yard at 4 inches covers 81 sq ft, and 500 / 81 = 6.17 yards, which matches step 4.

On cost, 7 yards at a mid price of $30 per yard is $210 for material, plus one delivery fee. The same volume in bags, 123 bags, would fill a car many times over and cost far more per yard. Past one yard, bulk is the right call almost every time. If the next job is a new lawn on this soil, pair this page with our [sod calculator](/blog/sod-calculator/) or a seed plan once the soil is spread and leveled.

## How deep should topsoil be?

Depth depends on what will grow in it. Use this guide:

| Job | Depth to use |
| --- | --- |
| Topdressing an existing lawn | 0.25 to 0.5 in |
| New lawn from seed or sod | 4 to 6 in |
| Flower beds | 6 to 8 in |
| Vegetable beds | 8 to 12 in |
| Filling a low spot | fill depth plus 10 percent for settling |

Thin soil is the false saving on lawn jobs. Grass roots in 2 inches of topsoil over hard clay dry out fast in July. If the soil under your job is decent loam, you can work compost into the top few inches and use less new topsoil. If it is pure clay or builder rubble, hold the full 4 to 6 inches. For raised beds, the same formula works: a 4 x 8 ft bed filled 12 inches deep needs 32 cu ft, which is 1.19 cubic yards.

Measure each area apart if depths differ. Sketch the yard, write the depth next to each part, and add the cubic yards at the end. Our [gravel calculator](/blog/gravel-calculator/) uses the same sketch method for paths.

## Bulk bags or a loose load?

Bags suit small jobs: a patch repair, a few planters, or one short bed. They are clean and store in a garage. The price per yard is high, often several times the bulk price.

Bulk loose loads suit anything over one cubic yard. Plan the drop spot before you order, and put a tarp on the driveway to keep cleanup short. Ask if the soil is screened. Screened soil has rocks and roots sifted out and spreads far faster by rake. Unscreened soil is cheaper and is fine for deep fill, with screened soil on top for planting.

One cubic yard of dry topsoil weighs roughly a ton or more. A half-ton pickup can carry about half a yard per trip safely, which is why delivery makes sense even for two or three yards.

## Common mistakes to avoid

Do not order by weight when the supplier sells by volume. Tons and yards are not the same unit, and wet soil weighs more per yard than dry soil. Order in cubic yards and confirm the truck box size if you doubt a load.

Do not forget settling and grading loss. Soil spread on a rough surface fills dips you did not measure. The 10 percent extra in the worked example is real, and running half a yard short means a second delivery fee for a small load.

Do not use fill dirt as topsoil. Fill dirt is subsoil with little organic matter. It is fine to build up grade deep down, but plants need real topsoil in the top 4 to 6 inches. If you are raising a low area by a foot, use fill for the bottom part and topsoil for the top part, much like the base layers in our [paver calculator](/blog/paver-calculator/).

Do not spread topsoil over weeds. Kill or strip old growth first, rough up the surface, then spread.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many bags of topsoil are in a cubic yard?
It depends on bag size. A cubic yard is 27 cu ft, so it is 18 bags at 1.5 cu ft, 27 bags at 1 cu ft, or 36 bags at 0.75 cu ft.

### How much topsoil do I need for 1,000 sq ft?
At 1 inch deep you need about 3.1 cubic yards. At 4 inches deep you need about 12.3 cubic yards. Multiply area by depth in feet and divide by 27.

### How much does a cubic yard of topsoil cost?
HomeGuide puts topsoil at $10 to $50 per cubic yard, based on type and quality, with delivery charged per load on top. Screened and blended soils sit at the high end.

### How deep should topsoil be under a new lawn?
Use 4 to 6 inches. That depth gives roots room to grow down and hold water. Less than 4 inches over poor subsoil often leads to a thin lawn that fades in heat.

### Should I buy topsoil in bags or bulk?
Buy bags under about a quarter yard. Buy bulk at one yard or more. The worked example job at 7 yards would take 123 bags, which is a clear bulk job.
